## Summary

Subagents investigating timing-dependent test failures spawn CPU saturation
workers (`python -c "while True: pass"`) to reproduce failures under load. Nothing
bounds their lifetime or reaps them. On this host **38 such workers** spawned in a
single batch on **2026-08-22 10:02:11**, orphaned to PID 1, and ran continuously
for **four days** at ~**1341% combined CPU** until manually killed on 2026-08-26.

## Evidence (observed 2026-08-26)

- 38 processes matching `python -c "\nwhile True: pass\n"`, each ~35–45% CPU.
- Every one had **PPID 1** — the spawning harness exited without reaping them.
- All shared start timestamp `Aug 22 10:02:11` — one batch, never cleaned up.
- Combined CPU 1341% on an 18-core host with only **6 performance cores**.
- Contributed to a load average of **58.49**; after `pkill -f 'while True: pass'`
  load fell to 26 and then to ~10.
- Applications could not launch while this was running (dock bounce, no window).
  Killing the workers restored launch.

## Provenance — which sessions, and why

Traced to three Claude Code sessions' subagent transcripts under
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-joeoakhart-rebar/`. Their own task descriptions state
the intent:

| Session | Recorded task description |
|---|---|
| `e50ec61e-3a77-4eb8-b56b-c1d0f90ff9bc` | "Reproduce crash on pristine main under saturating load"; "Run crashing tests under CPU pressure with repo ini budget" |
| `6f8df6b5-44f6-4ea4-b224-1eac4c95b0a7` | "Measure test runtime unloaded"; "Measure runtime under CPU pressure" |
| `eff19c3d-071a-47b5-bae6-8b48a3343a8c` | "Watch socket + CPU time over 50s"; "Per-thread CPU and leaf summary" |

This lines up with the `debug-ci-timeout` and `debug/ci-hang-99pct` worktrees.
Saturating the CPU to reproduce a timing-dependent failure is a legitimate
technique — the defect is that the workers outlive the investigation.

`while True: pass` appears **nowhere in the rebar codebase** (verified by grep over
`*.py`/`*.sh`/`*.md`). These were ad-hoc `python -c` invocations, so no repo-side
fixture is responsible and no repo-side change alone can prevent recurrence.

## Why it went unnoticed

- The workers are `nice`d (`RN`/`SN` state), so they yield rather than freeze the
  UI outright. Degradation is gradual and reads as "the machine feels slow."
- PPID-1 orphans have no session affinity — nothing associates them with the
  finished investigation that created them.
- No sweep exists for long-lived compute processes with no parent.

## Impact

- Four days of a workstation running at ~3x oversubscription.
- Compounded with an unrelated `fseventsd` blowup (see related ticket) to exhaust
  swap and block application launch entirely.
- Any timing-sensitive test run during that window produced unreliable results —
  including, plausibly, the CI-timing investigations that spawned the load.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Agent guidance (`AGENTS.md`) states that any background load generator or
      long-running helper a subagent spawns must be bounded in wall-clock time AT
      SPAWN, not merely killed at the end. Verified by the text being present in
      `AGENTS.md`.
- [ ] The guidance gives a copy-pasteable bounded pattern (for example
      `timeout 120 python -c '...' &`) and a process-group teardown
      (`trap 'kill 0' EXIT INT TERM`), with one line on why an unbounded loop
      outlives harness death. Verified by those literals appearing in `AGENTS.md`.
- [ ] The guidance forbids leaving PPID-1 orphans: a subagent reaps what it spawned
      before returning, including on error paths. Verified by the text in `AGENTS.md`.
- [ ] A detection check reports compute processes whose parent is PID 1 and whose
      accumulated CPU time exceeds **3600 CPU-seconds by default**, overridable via a
      `--min-cpu-seconds` argument. 3600 is chosen because the leaked generators had
      accumulated roughly 138,000 CPU-seconds (38 processes x ~40% CPU x 4 days) while
      a legitimate orphan rarely passes an hour of CPU. Runnable on demand as a plain
      command with no dependency on any CI provider (`project.portability`). Verified
      by `python scripts/check_orphaned_load.py --help` exiting 0.
- [ ] The check flags a bounded decoy process it is given and does NOT flag a
      normally-parented process. Verified by
      `pytest tests/scripts/test_check_orphaned_load.py`.
- [ ] The check's process-inspection seam is injectable so the test never depends on
      real system process state or on spawning a real long-lived CPU burner. Spawning
      a real unbounded CPU burner in a test would reproduce the very defect this
      ticket tracks. Verified by the same test module passing deterministically.
- [ ] The real (non-injected) adapter is exercised at least once against live process
      state in a READ-ONLY smoke assertion — it returns a list without raising, and
      the current process is not reported. This covers the parsing path the injected
      seam bypasses. Verified by that test in the same module.
- [ ] An operator note documents how to reclaim an already-leaked batch
      (`pkill -f 'while True: pass'` cleared this host's 38), and where the guidance
      lives. Verified by the note being present in `AGENTS.md`.

## Testing

- `pytest tests/scripts/test_check_orphaned_load.py` — the check flags an orphaned
  high-CPU process, ignores a normally-parented one, ignores a short-lived orphan
  below the CPU threshold, and honours the threshold argument.
- `make lint` and `make typecheck` — green.
- `python scripts/check_complexity_baseline.py --check` and
  `python scripts/check_import_walk.py` — green.

## Definition of Done

- Guidance merged in the canonical agent file, not only in a machine-local note.
- Detection check implemented and covered by the test in AC 5.
- A short operator note on reclaiming an already-leaked batch
  (`pkill -f 'while True: pass'` was sufficient here, but the general form should be
  documented).

## Notes

Found while triaging a host-wide starvation incident. Two independent resource
leaks — this one and unbounded gate-snapshot accumulation driving `fseventsd` —
compounded to make the machine unusable. They are separate defects with separate
fixes; this ticket tracks the orphaned-load-generator half.

Remediation already applied on this host: `pkill -f 'while True: pass'` (38 killed,
0 remaining, load 58 -> 10). Nothing respawns them; the batch was a one-time leak.
